lines.text: From holes drilled in Stone Age skulls to vaccines made in under a year, this is the long story of how we came to understand the body and learned to heal it.
Some eight thousand years ago, people were already cutting holes in living skulls. Many of those skulls healed, so patients survived this first known operation.
In Egypt, Imhotep built the first pyramid, and later generations honoured him as a god of medicine and healing.
An Egyptian scroll from about 1600 BCE describes wounds and how to treat them. It is the oldest surgical text we know.
Soon after, another Egyptian scroll gathered hundreds of remedies and spells, one of the oldest medical books to survive.
Meanwhile a deadly virus was spreading among people. Smallpox would scar and kill hundreds of millions over the next three thousand years.
In ancient India, the Sushruta Samhita described surgery in detail, including operations to rebuild a damaged nose.
In Greece, Hippocrates taught that illness has natural causes, found by careful watching. He is still called the father of medicine.
Then disease struck Athens itself during its war with Sparta, killing a great share of the crowded city, its leader Pericles among them.
Doctors began draining blood to restore the body's balance. The practice lasted more than two thousand years, and it rarely helped.
From the same Greek world came the Hippocratic Oath, a promise of ethics that new doctors still echo today.
In China, the Yellow Emperor's Classic laid the foundations of traditional Chinese medicine, written as conversations between a ruler and his ministers.
From that tradition came acupuncture, fine needles placed at points on the body. It is used worldwide now, though its effects are still debated.
In the Roman world, Galen treated gladiators and emperors. His ideas, drawn from animal dissection and the four humours, ruled medicine for some fifteen centuries.
In his lifetime, soldiers returning from the East brought a great epidemic, perhaps smallpox, that swept through Rome's cities and armies.
Less than a century later another epidemic struck the empire, in a time already torn by war and unrest.
In 541 the first true plague in recorded history reached Constantinople, and it came back in waves for two hundred years.
In Baghdad, the Persian physician al-Razi ran hospitals and became the first to tell smallpox and measles apart.
His careful account of measles, a fiercely contagious fever with a rash, would stand for centuries until a vaccine came in the sixties.
Not long after, another Persian, Avicenna, became one of the great physicians and philosophers of his age.
Across Asia, Africa and the Ottoman lands, people learned to give a mild dose of smallpox on purpose, so that they would become immune.
Avicenna's Canon of Medicine gathered Greek and Islamic learning into one huge book, taught in European schools for hundreds of years.
In the 1340s the Black Death crossed Asia and Europe, killing a vast share of the people it reached and changing work, wages and faith.
After 1492, ships carried crops and animals across the Atlantic, and diseases too. Smallpox killed huge numbers of Indigenous Americans.
In Europe, Andreas Vesalius did something bold: he dissected human bodies with his own hands and looked for himself.
His great illustrated book of 1543 corrected many of Galen's mistakes and founded modern anatomy.
Meanwhile in Mexico, two waves of a terrible fever killed a huge share of the native population. Its cause is still debated.
In England, William Harvey showed that the heart pumps blood round the body in a circuit, overturning ideas that went back to the Greeks.
Armies of the Thirty Years' War carried plague into northern Italy, and cities like Milan and Venice lost a great part of their people.
From the Andes came quinine, from the bark of the cinchona tree. For centuries it was the main treatment for malaria.
A Dutch cloth merchant ground tiny, powerful lenses, and Antonie van Leeuwenhoek became the first person to see bacteria.
In 1665 plague returned to London one last time, emptying the city of the rich and sealing up the houses of the sick.
That same year, Robert Hooke's drawings through the microscope gave a name to the cell.
In 1720 a ship brought plague to Marseille, in one of the last great outbreaks in western Europe.
Then an English country doctor, Edward Jenner, noticed that cowpox protected people from smallpox, and in 1796 he put it to the test.
A few years earlier, yellow fever had swept through Philadelphia, then the American capital. Much later the blame fell on mosquitoes.
Jenner's discovery became the very first vaccine, the weapon that would one day end smallpox for good.
In 1816 a French doctor rolled up paper to listen to a patient's chest, and the stethoscope was born.
Two years later a British doctor made the first successful transfusion of blood between people, though it would long remain risky.
In the Crimean War, Florence Nightingale used numbers to show how dirt killed the wounded, and she made nursing a profession.
In France, Louis Pasteur showed that germs cause disease, and he went on to make vaccines and give us pasteurisation.
Inspired by germs, Joseph Lister cleaned wounds and instruments with carbolic acid, and deaths after surgery fell sharply.
Cholera spread from India along trade routes to Europe and the Americas, and frightened cities began to build sewers and clean water supplies.
In Germany, Robert Koch proved that each disease has its own germ, finding the bacteria of anthrax, tuberculosis and cholera.
In Boston in 1846, a patient breathed ether and slept through an operation, and surgery no longer had to be a race against pain.
A few years later the hollow needle and syringe made injections of painkillers, and later vaccines, an everyday thing.
In London in 1854, John Snow mapped a cholera outbreak to a single water pump, a landmark in tracing how disease spreads.
Plague set out once more from China, riding steamships to ports around the world, until researchers in Hong Kong found its bacterium.
In Vienna, Sigmund Freud began treating the troubled mind by talking, and his ideas about the unconscious spread far, though many are disputed.
By the 1860s germ theory was taking hold: many diseases are caused by microbes, and that idea led to clean surgery, vaccines and antibiotics.
In Geneva, the Red Cross was founded to care for wounded soldiers, prisoners and civilians in war.
Marie Curie discovered radium and polonium, won Nobel Prizes in two sciences, and sent X-ray units to the front in the First World War.
Born in Scotland in 1881, Alexander Fleming would one day notice a mould that killed bacteria, and change medicine forever.
In 1885 Pasteur gave his new rabies vaccine to a boy bitten by a rabid dog, and the boy lived.
Ten years later, Wilhelm Roentgen found rays that passed through flesh but not bone, and within months doctors could see inside the body.
Then came aspirin, from a compound in willow bark, a simple painkiller that is still in almost every home.
In 1901, Karl Landsteiner found the A, B and O blood groups, and at last transfusions could be made safe.
As the First World War ended, a flu pandemic swept the world, infecting a huge share of humanity and killing many young adults.
In Toronto in 1922, insulin was given to a patient for the first time, and diabetes stopped being a death sentence.
For children paralysed by polio, the iron lung, a metal tank around the body, breathed for them and kept them alive.
In 1928 Fleming's mouldy dish revealed penicillin. Made into a drug in the forties, it began the age of antibiotics.
Not every new treatment was a step forward. Lobotomy, cutting into the brain to treat mental illness, harmed many patients and was abandoned.
In the forties, doctors began treating cancer with drugs that kill dividing cells. Chemotherapy had begun.
During the Second World War, the Dutch doctor Willem Kolff built a machine to clean the blood when the kidneys fail.
In 1948 the World Health Organization was founded in Geneva, to work for the health of the whole world.
In 1953 the structure of DNA was revealed as a double helix, showing how the instructions of life are copied.
Two years later Jonas Salk's polio vaccine was approved, and the disease that paralysed children began to retreat.
Then came a warning. Thalidomide, given for morning sickness, harmed unborn babies, and new medicines faced much stricter testing.
In 1957 a new flu from East Asia circled the globe within months, and vaccines were made while it spread.
A year later in Sweden, doctors placed the first pacemaker in a patient's chest, a small device to keep the heart beating steadily.
In the early sixties the pill gave women a reliable way to plan their families, and it changed daily life.
In Cape Town in 1967, Christiaan Barnard gave a patient a new heart, the first human heart transplant.
The next year another flu, first seen in Hong Kong, spread around the world. It was milder than 1918, but still deadly for the old.
In the early seventies, the CT scanner built pictures of slices of the body from many X-rays, letting doctors see inside the head.
In 1977 came the first MRI scan of a human body, using magnets and radio waves instead of X-rays.
A year later Louise Brown was born in England, the first baby conceived in a laboratory dish. Millions have followed.
And in 1980 came a triumph: smallpox was declared gone, the only human disease ever wiped out.
Soon after, a new virus that weakens the body's defences was reported. HIV spread worldwide, until medicines let people live long lives.
In 1990 scientists set out to read every letter of human DNA, and by 2003 the Human Genome Project was done.
Along the way, in Scotland, Dolly the sheep was born, the first mammal cloned from an adult cell.
In 2002 a new coronavirus, SARS, spread by air travel, but it was contained within months.
In 2009 a new flu from Mexico went worldwide. It was milder than feared, but it tested the world's plans.
In 2012 scientists showed that CRISPR, borrowed from bacteria, could cut DNA at chosen places. Genes could now be edited.
The next year, the largest Ebola outbreak ever began in Guinea, taking many health workers and spurring new ways to test vaccines.
Then the Zika virus, carried by mosquitoes, spread through Brazil and the Americas and was linked to birth defects.
A new drug, semaglutide, made first for diabetes, went on to change how obesity is treated.
Then in early 2020 a new coronavirus brought the world to a halt, with lockdowns, closed schools and years of disruption.
Within a year came a new kind of vaccine, mRNA, teaching the body's own cells to recognise the virus.
In 2021 the first malaria vaccine was approved for children in Africa, against one of humanity's oldest killers.
And in 2023 came Casgevy, the first medicine made with gene editing, able to cure sickle cell disease.
From skull surgery to gene editing, every step was learned the hard way, one body at a time.
